source.title: Andhra Pradesh High Court on Passport Denial Based on FIR
source.description:
Can your passport be denied just because an FIR has been filed against you?

The Andhra Pradesh High Court held that the answer is no.

The Court clarified that a mere FIR or pending police investigation is not enough to refuse a passport. Under the Passports Act, a passport can be denied only when criminal proceedings are pending before a competent court.

The judgment also reiterates that the right to travel abroad forms part of personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution.

{Andhra Pradesh High Court, Passport, FIR, Passports Act, Article 21, Right to travel, Criminal proceedings, Personal liberty, Legal updates, IndiaLaw}

#IndiaLaw #Passport #Article21 #AndhraPradeshHighCourt #LegalAwareness

source.title: Death Does Not Discharge Debt: Bombay HC on Maintenance
source.description:
A maintenance decree does not automatically end with the husband’s death.

The Bombay High Court held that existing maintenance arrears and the amount fixed under a decree can be recovered from the deceased husband’s estate. However, a divorced wife cannot seek enhancement after his death, as the personal obligation to maintain ends with him.

Death may not erase the decree, but it limits any fresh claim for increased maintenance.

{Maintenance decree, divorced wife rights, Bombay High Court, maintenance after death, family law}

#MaintenanceLaw #BombayHighCourt #FamilyLaw #DivorceLaw #LegalRights #IndiaLaw #LegalUpdate

source.title: Rajasthan High Court on Employer-Employee Relationship Under the Workmen’s Compensation Act
source.description:
Can a family receive employee compensation without proving that the deceased actually worked there?

The Rajasthan High Court held that the answer is no.

In this case, there were no salary records, appointment letters, attendance records, or wage slips to establish an employer-employee relationship. The Court also clarified that taking an injured person to the hospital is an act of humanity and by itself, does not prove employment.

Since the employer-employee relationship was not established, the Court set aside the compensation award.

{Rajasthan High Court, Workmen's Compensation Act, Employer-employee relationship, Employee compensation, Labour law, Compensation claim, Evidence, Legal updates, IndiaLaw}

#IndiaLaw #LabourLaw #RajasthanHighCourt #EmployeeCompensation #LegalAwareness

source.title: Reinstatement cannot rest on unsupported claims alone.
source.description:
In M/s Rifilis Engineering Pvt. Ltd. v. Arjun Gupta, the Supreme Court held that an employee seeking reinstatement must produce reliable evidence to justify unauthorised absence or prove an attempt to rejoin. The Court therefore set aside the order granting reinstatement and back wages.

In labour disputes, the burden of proof matters. Oral assertions without supporting evidence may not be enough.

{Unauthorised absence, reinstatement, back wages, burden of proof, Supreme Court labour law}

#LabourLaw #SupremeCourt #EmploymentLaw #BackWages #Reinstatement #IndiaLaw #LegalUpdate

source.title: Can every professional fee be recognised as a CIRP cost?
source.description:
In Prateek S Jain & Associates v. Pratim Bayal, the NCLT Kolkata examined a GST consultant’s claim for ₹6.48 lakh in unpaid fees during the CIRP of Nandini Impex.

While GST compliance services may qualify as CIRP costs under Section 5(13) of the IBC, the Tribunal emphasised that such costs must be necessary, reasonable, and proportionate to the work performed. With limited business activity and predominantly Nil GST returns, the fees claimed were found excessive.

The ruling highlights the importance of proportionality in recognising professional fees as CIRP costs, even when statutory priority is involved.

{CIRP Costs, IBC Section 5(13), NCLT Kolkata, GST Consultant Fees, Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, Professional Fees, Insolvency Law}

#CIRP #IBC #NCLT #InsolvencyLaw #IndiaLaw

source.title: Supreme Court on DNA Testing in Paternity Disputes
source.description:
Can a court compel someone to undergo a DNA test in a paternity dispute?

The Supreme Court held that DNA tests cannot be ordered routinely. Courts must first determine whether there is an eminent need for the test and whether other evidence can resolve the dispute.

In Chaturbhuj Pradhan v. Amar Pradhan & Anr., the Court balanced the right to privacy with the right to establish parentage and inheritance. Finding that no other evidence could conclusively determine paternity, it upheld the direction to undergo DNA testing.

The ruling reinforces that DNA testing is an exceptional remedy, permitted only when justice truly requires it.

{Supreme Court, DNA testing, Paternity dispute, Parentage, Right to privacy, Inheritance, Civil law, Evidence, Legal updates, IndiaLaw}

#IndiaLaw #SupremeCourt #DNATest #Paternity #LegalAwareness

source.title: Minor Victims Cannot Waive Justice: Rajasthan High Court Reaffirms POSCO Protections
source.description:
A minor victim cannot waive the protections guaranteed under the POCSO Act.

The Rajasthan High Court held that a minor’s consent or later “no objection” cannot by itself justify closing proceedings in a POCSO case. The Court also stressed the importance of proper guardian representation and legal assistance under Section 40 of the Act.

POCSO safeguards cannot be bypassed merely because a minor later chooses not to pursue the case.

{POCSO Act, minor victim rights, Section 40 POCSO, Rajasthan High Court, child protection law}

#POCSO #ChildProtection #RajasthanHighCourt #CriminalLaw #LegalRights #IndiaLaw #LegalUpdate

source.title: CCPA Fines PhysicsWallah for Dark Patterns
source.description:
Can a pre-ticked donation box during online checkout violate consumer law?

The CCPA held that the answer is yes.

PhysicsWallah was fined ₹5 lakh for using dark patterns, including a pre-selected donation checkbox, emotional prompts encouraging donations, and requiring users to share personal details to access ""free"" courses.

The Authority clarified that valid digital consent must be affirmative, informed, and voluntary. A pre-ticked checkbox is not valid consent.

The ruling reinforces that online platforms cannot use design tricks to influence consumer choices.

{CCPA, PhysicsWallah, Dark patterns, Consumer protection, Digital consent, Basket sneaking, Confirm shaming, EdTech, Legal updates, IndiaLaw}

#IndiaLaw #ConsumerProtection #DarkPatterns #CCPA #LegalAwareness

source.title: Adoption procedure cannot be applied so rigidly that it defeats the welfare of the child
source.description:
In Ms. Karnika Khandelwal v. Union of India, the Delhi High Court held that CARA could not insist on a procedural requirement that was practically impossible to fulfil in an OCI-parent HAMA adoption involving Australia. The Court instead directed verification under Regulation 69, followed by issuance of the NOC.

In adoption matters, procedure must ultimately serve the child’s welfare, not obstruct it.

{HAMA adoption, CARA NOC, OCI parents, Delhi High Court, child welfare, expatriate adoption}

#AdoptionLaw #HAMA #CARA #DelhiHighCourt #ChildWelfare #FamilyLaw #IndiaLaw #LegalUpdate

source.title: Supreme Court on Contempt and Elephant Welfare
source.description:
Can breaking a promise made to the Supreme Court lead to contempt proceedings?

The Supreme Court answered yes in a case involving a captive elephant named Raman.

After finding that an undertaking given to the Court regarding the elephant's welfare had been violated, the Court held the respondent guilty of contempt, imposed a fine, and directed the Kerala authorities to take temporary custody of Raman for his protection.

The ruling reinforces that an undertaking given before the Supreme Court is legally binding, especially where animal welfare is at stake.

{Supreme Court, Contempt of court, Animal welfare, Captive elephant, Raman elephant, Undertaking, Kerala, Legal updates, IndiaLaw}

#IndiaLaw #SupremeCourt #AnimalWelfare #ContemptOfCourt #LegalAwareness

source.title: Mere Change in Project Name Cannot Defeat Statutory Rights of Home Buyers
source.description:
A project’s name may change, but home buyers’ statutory rights do not.

In *Shakti Anand v. Sahyog Homes Ltd.*, the Maharashtra Real Estate Appellate Tribunal held that a project is identified by its underlying land and sanctioned permissions, not merely its marketing name. Buyers of “BBJ Roma” were therefore recognised as allottees of the registered “Verona” project and entitled to RERA protection.

Changing the project name cannot be used to defeat home buyers’ rights under RERA.

{RERA rights, home buyers protection, project name change, MahaRERA, real estate law}

#RERA #HomeBuyers #RealEstateLaw #MahaRERA #PropertyLaw #IndiaLaw #LegalUpdate

source.title: Form F compliance under the PCPNDT Act is not merely a procedural formality.
source.description:
In Dr. Ramesh v. State of Maharashtra, the Supreme Court reaffirmed that deficiencies in mandatory Form F records can attract prosecution. The Court stressed that these records play a crucial role in monitoring prenatal diagnostic procedures and preventing illegal sex determination.

Under the PCPNDT Act, strict statutory record-keeping is essential, and claims of clerical error must be tested during trial.

{PCPNDT Act, Form F compliance, Supreme Court, prenatal diagnostics, sex determination law}

#PCPNDTAct #SupremeCourt #MedicalLaw #HealthcareLaw #LegalCompliance #IndiaLaw #LegalUpdate

source.title: An arbitration clause cannot be invoked indefinitely.
source.description:
In IDFC First Bank Ltd. v. Shyamsundar Distributor, the Calcutta High Court held that a Section 8 application must be filed within the period available for submitting the written statement. An unexplained delay of nearly 11 months was therefore held to be time-barred.

In arbitration disputes, delay can amount to waiver of the right to seek reference to arbitration.

{Section 8 Arbitration Act, arbitration clause, Calcutta High Court, limitation, civil proceedings}

#ArbitrationLaw #Section8 #CalcuttaHighCourt #DisputeResolution #CivilLaw #IndiaLaw #LegalUpdate

source.title: Under SARFAESI proceedings, the borrower’s right of redemption does not remain open indefinitely.
source.description:
In Khaja Moideen Leather Company v. Authorised Officer, Indian Bank, the DRAT Chennai reiterated that the right to redeem the secured property is extinguished once the sale notice is published. Payment of outstanding dues after that stage does not automatically restore the borrower’s right to reclaim the property.

In recovery proceedings, timing can determine whether the right of redemption survives.

{SARFAESI Act, right of redemption, DRAT Chennai, property auction, secured assets}

#SARFAESI #BankingLaw #DRAT #PropertyAuction #DebtRecovery #IndiaLaw #LegalUpdate

source.title: Delhi High Court on Personality Rights and Deepfakes
source.description:
Actor Naga Chaitanya's identity was allegedly misused through AI-generated deepfakes. What did the Delhi High Court say?

The Delhi High Court observed that a person's identity carries both commercial value and personal dignity. It noted that AI tools, deepfakes, and face morphing technology can seriously harm an individual's reputation and mislead the public.

The Court restrained the unauthorized use of Naga Chaitanya's name, image, voice, likeness, and persona, and directed the removal of infringing content.

The ruling reinforces that personality rights extend to the digital world, and unauthorized use of someone's identity through AI or deepfakes can have legal consequences.

{Delhi High Court, Personality rights, Deepfakes, Artificial Intelligence, AI, Naga Chaitanya, Digital rights, Face morphing, Intellectual Property, Legal updates, IndiaLaw}

#IndiaLaw #Deepfakes #PersonalityRights #AI #LegalAwareness

source.title: The right to walk safely is a fundamental right.
source.description:
In Maniyar Iliyaz Shaik Riyaz v. P. Ayyappan, the Supreme Court held that safe, demarcated footpaths fall within the protection of Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution. The Court also stressed that municipal bodies and local authorities have a duty to provide and maintain proper pedestrian infrastructure.

Roads are for people too, not just vehicles. Pedestrian safety is a constitutional responsibility.

{Right to walk, Article 19, Article 21, Supreme Court pedestrian rights, footpath safety}

#RightToWalk #Article21 #SupremeCourt #PedestrianSafety #IndiaLaw #LegalUpdate

source.title: An adult’s right to choose their partner cannot be overridden by social convention.
source.description:
In Ridham Verma & Others v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Others, the Madhya Pradesh High Court held that two consenting adults have the right to live together even outside marriage. The Court recognised such a choice as an exercise of personal liberty protected under Article 21.

Family or societal pressure cannot take away an adult’s freedom to choose companionship.

{Live-in relationship, Article 21, personal liberty, adult choice, Madhya Pradesh High Court}

#LiveInRelationship #Article21 #PersonalLiberty #ConstitutionalRights #FamilyLaw #IndiaLaw #LegalUpdate
